culture: Ballarò is a famous, lively street market in Palermo, Sicily, full of voices and colors
Pane con la milza (spleen sandwich) is a traditional Palermo street food
The spleen is cooked slowly in strutto (lard)
Spleen sandwiches come 'schietta' (plain) or 'maritata' (married), meaning with ricotta and caciocavallo cheese
Caciocavallo is a stretched-curd Italian cheese
Panelle are Sicilian chickpea fritters, eaten hot and put straight into the bread
Lemon is often squeezed on panelle and the sandwich
Spleen is traditionally eaten hot
Saturday is the busiest market day, when families come to shop and panelle sell out ('vanno a ruba')
Many street food vendors learn the trade from their fathers and start working as children
Italian phrase 'andare a ruba' means to sell like hotcakes
Common vendor greetings and farewells: 'Ci vediamo sabato', 'Buona giornata', 'buon appetito', 'a presto'
'Favorite' is a vendor's polite call to invite customers to come and take food
Italian phrase 'come si deve' means 'the proper way'

culture: Pane e milza (pani ca meusa) is a Palermo street-food sandwich of spleen served in a bun
Ballarò is a historic open-air market in Palermo, Sicily
Milza is the Italian word for spleen
Strutto means lard, traditionally used for frying the spleen
Schietta means plain: the sandwich has just spleen and lemon
Maritata means married: the sandwich is topped with ricotta and caciocavallo cheese
Ricotta and caciocavallo are Italian cheeses used in the maritata sandwich
Panelle are fried chickpea-flour fritters made with chickpea flour, water and salt
Panelle are eaten inside the bread with a squeeze of lemon
Palermitans (palermitani) are people from Palermo
Market vendors work very early, from around 4 a.m., to prepare fresh food
Market stalls and vendors form a close-knit community where everyone knows each other
Food trades are often passed down in families, from father to son
Italian proverb-style sayings are common: hot bread waits for no one
Friggitoria means a fry shop that sells fried street food
Italians use formal Lei with customers and strangers, and informal ti with familiar people
Common phrases: buon appetito, a presto, a sabato, buona giornata, stammi bene
Meno male means thank goodness

culture: The Sassi di Matera are unique in the world
The Sassi are ancient cave dwellings carved into the rock
The Civita is the oldest part of the Sassi, the old hill at its heart
People used to live in cave houses (case-grotta) in the Sassi
Cave houses stayed warm in winter and cool in summer
Cave houses were often a single room where the whole family slept together, even with the donkey
Donkeys were kept in the home and used to fetch water from the fountain
The Sassi have stairways with smooth stones that require walking carefully
The Sassi include rock churches (chiese rupestri) as well as cave houses
Italian greeting: Buon pomeriggio (good afternoon)
Italian phrase: A domani (see you tomorrow)
Italian word: ciao used as a farewell
Italian phrase: Buona passeggiata (enjoy your walk)

culture: Matera's Sassi are ancient cave dwellings where many people were born and lived, including Giovanni
The Civita is the old part of Matera's Sassi, which glows golden at sunset
Families in the Sassi once lived in one room together with animals such as chickens and a mule
Life in the Sassi was hard but warm, close-knit and communal, with neighbors like one family and evening singing
The idiom 'un pezzo di pane' (a piece of bread) means a very kind, good-hearted person
Matera's bread is famous throughout Italy
Bread can be bought at a local bakery (fornaio), such as on via del Corso, ideally a warm loaf (pagnotta)
Italian greetings and farewells: Buon pomeriggio, A domani, Ciao ciao
Locals have a custom of sitting daily to admire the view and sharing stories with visitors
Useful words: grotta (cave), tramonto (sunset), vicini (neighbors), fornaio (baker), pagnotta (loaf), casa (home)
